record.original_question: In classical gravity, is Newton's inverse-distance gravitational potential really valid at galactic and larger distance scales, or can observations admit a non-Newtonian large-distance potential such as a linear potential term? This question includes whether flat HI galactic rotation curves should be interpreted as evidence for unobserved dark matter within Newton-Einstein gravity or as evidence that the simple Newtonian 1/r potential is being applied outside the distance range where it has been established.

evidence.quote: On the observational side we discuss the degree to which the realm of validity of Newton’s Law of Gravity can actually be extended to distances much larger than the solar system distance scales on which the law was originally established.

Thus we need to ask whether the potential really is 1/r on much larger distance scales, and whether universal coupling actually necessitates the introduction of the fundamental constant G in the first place.

Thus it would appear to us that at the present time one cannot categorically assert that the sole gravitational potential on all distance scales is the Newtonian one, and that, in the linear potential, the standard 1/r potential would not only appear to have a companion but to have one which would even dominate over it asymptotically.

Indeed, the very need for dark matter in the standard theory may simply be due to trying to apply just the simple Newtonian potential in a domain for which there is no prior (or even current for that matter) justification.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider classical gravitation in the weak-field, non-relativistic regime, where the gravitational potential generated by a static mass distribution is conventionally taken to be the Newtonian potential V(r) = -GM/r, established empirically on solar-system distance scales. Let the observed (approximately flat) HI rotation curves of spiral galaxies at large galactocentric radii serve as test data.

(a) Determine whether the gravitational potential of a localized mass distribution must, on galactic and larger distance scales, be exactly Newtonian (i.e. proportional to 1/r for a point mass), or whether observations are equally consistent with a modified large-distance potential of the form
   V(r) = -GM/r + γ M r
(an additional linear-in-r term, with γ a universal coupling), or with another non-Newtonian asymptotic behavior.

(b) Decide whether the observed flatness of galactic rotation curves should be regarded as evidence for the existence of unseen ("dark") matter distributed in halos within standard Newton–Einstein gravity, or instead as evidence that the 1/r potential is being extrapolated beyond the range of distances on which it has been empirically validated, with the asymptotic dynamics actually governed by a non-Newtonian (e.g. linear) term.

State definitively, with theoretical and observational justification, which alternative is correct, or prove that current data cannot discriminate between them.
artifact.status_search_result: The question of whether Newtonian gravity needs modification at galactic scales or whether flat rotation curves require dark matter remains actively debated. Recent (2022–2025) work continues to explore conformal-gravity-type linear potentials, MOND-like modifications, and f(R,T) theories as alternatives to dark matter, while also documenting tensions (e.g., strong lensing constraints on universal linear-potential parameters). No consensus resolution exists.

status_evidence.title: Distinguishing Dark Matter, Modified Gravity, and Modified Inertia with the Inner and Outer Parts of Galactic Rotation Curves
status_evidence.snippet: Modified gravity under an estimated mean external field correctly predicts the observed statistical relation of accelerations from both the inner and outer parts of rotation curves.
status_evidence.claim: Active research continues to compare dark matter and modified-gravity explanations of rotation curves.

status_evidence.title: Conformal gravity rotation curves and strong lensing (2025)
status_evidence.snippet: Conformal Gravity predicts an additional linear potential ... encounters difficulties remaining consistent with strong lensing observations.
status_evidence.claim: Linear-potential modifications to Newtonian gravity remain under active investigation with unresolved tensions.

status_evidence.title: The galaxy rotation curves in the f(R,T) modified gravity
status_evidence.snippet: f(R,T) modified gravity offers a resolution to flat rotation curve observations.
status_evidence.claim: Multiple alternative gravity proposals are still being developed to explain rotation curves without dark matter.
